title: ReDoS: when a regex takes down production
summary: Regex denial of service as a security bug, the Stack Overflow and Cloudflare outages, the defences in order, NonBacktracking and match timeouts in .NET, and the tools that find the stuck thread.

steps.title: ReDoS: a denial of service in one string
body: **ReDoS** (regular expression denial of service) needs two things: a pattern that can backtrack badly, and input an
attacker controls. One request pins a thread at 100% CPU; a handful pin every core. No exploit code, just text.
It is a real vulnerability class (CWE-1333) and dependency scanners file CVEs for it.
Two outages every senior has heard of:
- **Stack Overflow, 20 July 2016.** A post contained about 20,000 consecutive whitespace characters. The home page
ran a trim regex over it: `^[\s\u200c]+|[\s\u200c]+$` (shown below). The load balancer's health check hit the home
page, timed out, and took the web servers out of rotation. The site was down for 34 minutes. The fix was to
replace the regex with a plain trim loop.
- **Cloudflare, 2 July 2019.** A new WAF rule containing `.*(?:.*=.*)` was deployed to every edge server at once. CPU
went to 100% worldwide and Cloudflare served 502 errors for about 27 minutes. Afterwards they moved rule matching
to an engine with guaranteed linear time and changed rollouts to be staged.
Neither pattern looks dangerous. Both passed normal tests.

steps.prompt: Why was the Stack Overflow trim regex slow on 20,000 spaces followed by a letter?
options: At every start position inside the run, `[\s\u200c]+` ran to the end of the spaces and then `$` failed on the letter: about 20,000 × 20,000 / 2 = 200 million steps
The `|` makes the engine scan the input twice
steps.explain: This one is **quadratic**, not exponential: no nested quantifier, but an unanchored search retries at every position, and each retry rescans the rest of the run. Quadratic is enough: 20,000 characters became 200 million steps per page view. Watch for patterns that start with a variable-length run and fail at the end.

steps.title: Trailing whitespace, in linear time
prompt: Find the run of trailing whitespace (`\s` or U+200C, the zero-width non-joiner) at the end of the text, as one
match. The Stack Overflow version, `[\s\u200c]+$`, fails the check with 20,000 spaces and a letter.
Only start a match where the previous character is **not** whitespace, with a negative lookbehind `(?<!...)`. Then
only one position in the run is ever tried.

require.message: Uses a lookbehind to start only at the beginning of the run

hints: Put `(?<![\s\u200c])` in front of the starter.
steps.explain: Inside the run, every position fails the lookbehind in one step. Only the first space of the run starts a real attempt, so the whole scan is linear. In application code, `string.TrimEnd()` (or a loop) is simpler still, which is what Stack Overflow shipped.

steps.title: The defences, in order
body: 1. **Rewrite** so each character can be matched one way (previous lesson). This fixes the cause.
2. **Atomic groups** `(?>...)` where a rewrite is awkward.
3. **`RegexOptions.NonBacktracking`** (.NET 7+): a different engine built on finite automata. Matching time is linear
in the input length, whatever the pattern. The costs: no lookarounds, backreferences, atomic groups or conditionals
(the constructor throws `NotSupportedException`), construction is slower, and simple patterns can match a little
slower than with the backtracking engine.
4. **A match timeout, always, for untrusted input.** The default is `Regex.InfiniteMatchTimeout`. Set one per regex,
or once for the process at startup, before any regex is built:
```csharp fragment
var slug = new Regex(@"^[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*$", RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
AppContext.SetData("REGEX_DEFAULT_MATCH_TIMEOUT", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));   // process-wide default
try { ok = slug.IsMatch(input); }
catch (RegexMatchTimeoutException ex)
logger.LogWarning("Regex timed out after {Timeout} on {Length} chars", ex.MatchTimeout, input.Length);
ok = false;   // a safe answer: treat it as invalid
Log the pattern and the input **length**, not the input: it may be huge or personal data. And bound the input first
(a 32-character username field should never see 1 MB), although, as you will see, a length limit alone is not enough.

steps.explain: A backreference needs to remember what a group matched, which a finite automaton cannot do, so the constructor refuses it. The catastrophic pattern is harmless under NonBacktracking: it answers `False` in linear time, without trying splits at all.

steps.prompt: Constructing a regex with `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking`: does this construct work, or does it throw?
steps.explain: Captures still work, so most parsing patterns move over unchanged. Lookarounds, backreferences and atomic groups are the price of the linear-time guarantee (and atomic groups are pointless there anyway: nothing backtracks).

steps.title: Symptom: the signup API pegs a core
prompt: **Symptom.** Last Tuesday one request to `POST /signup` pinned a CPU core until the pod restarted. `dotnet-counters`
showed CPU at 100% with almost no requests completing, and a dump showed the hot thread here:
```text
System.Text.RegularExpressions.RegexInterpreter.TryMatchAtCurrentPosition
System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex.RunSingleMatch
Signup.Api.UsernameRules.IsValidUsername
The hotfix added a 100 ms timeout. Now that request returns **500** with an unhandled `RegexMatchTimeoutException`.
Fix `bool IsValidUsername(string name)` properly. The rule (product confirmed it): 3 to 32 characters, runs of ASCII
letters and digits joined by **single** underscores, no underscore at the start or end.
- Check the length first. It is cheap, but notice that it does not save you: the attack input is only 32 characters.
- Rewrite the pattern so it is linear, and end it with `\z` (`$` would let `ana\n` through).
- Keep the 100 ms timeout and catch `RegexMatchTimeoutException`, returning `false`, as a safety net.
starter: var username = new Regex(@"^([a-zA-Z0-9]+_?)+$", RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100));
template: using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
{{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("ana is valid", true, IsValidUsername("ana"));
Dojo.Eq("ana_b_2 is valid", true, IsValidUsername("ana_b_2"));
Dojo.Eq("32 characters is valid", true, IsValidUsername(new string('a', 32)));
Dojo.Eq("2 characters is too short", false, IsValidUsername("ab"));
Dojo.Eq("33 characters is too long", false, IsValidUsername(new string('a', 33)));
Dojo.Eq("a double underscore is refused", false, IsValidUsername("ana__b"));
Dojo.Eq("a leading underscore is refused", false, IsValidUsername("_ana"));
Dojo.Eq("a trailing underscore is refused", false, IsValidUsername("ana_"));
Dojo.Eq("a space is refused", false, IsValidUsername("ana b"));
Dojo.Eq("a trailing newline is refused", false, IsValidUsername("ana\n"));
Dojo.Try("the 32-character attack input (unhandled exception)", () => Dojo.Eq("the 32-character attack input is refused fast", false, IsValidUsername(new string('a', 31) + "!")));
hints: Pattern: one run, then repeat "an underscore and a run": `^[a-zA-Z0-9]+(?:_[a-zA-Z0-9]+)*\z`.
Wrap `return username.IsMatch(name);` in `try { ... } catch (RegexMatchTimeoutException) { return false; }`.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: finding and preventing a stuck regex
steps.body: When a .NET service is hot, these tell you which thread and which frame, without a debugger attached. Then the scanners keep the next vulnerable pattern out of main. Install the diagnostics with `dotnet tool install -g dotnet-counters` (likewise dotnet-dump, dotnet-trace).

toolkit.what: Live runtime counters for a running .NET process: CPU, GC, thread pool queue, exceptions. A ReDoS shows as CPU stuck high while the request rate drops and the thread pool queue grows.
flags: pick the process by name or by id (dotnet-counters ps lists them)
which counter sets to show, e.g. System.Runtime,Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting
toolkit.when: the first look when a service is slow or hot

toolkit.what: Snapshot every thread of the process, then read the stacks offline. A stuck regex is a thread sitting in System.Text.RegularExpressions frames under your own method.
flags: open the dump in an SOS shell
the managed stack of every thread
parallel stacks: identical stacks merged, so the hot one stands out
toolkit.when: a process is pegged or hung and you need to know where

toolkit.what: Sample where CPU time goes for 30 seconds. Open the .nettrace in Visual Studio or PerfView, or write Speedscope format for speedscope.app.
flags: stop on its own after this long
a file speedscope.app can open in the browser
toolkit.when: CPU is high but not stuck, and you want the hot path

toolkit.what: BenchmarkDotNet, the standard .NET micro-benchmark library: warm-up, many iterations, mean and error. A Stopwatch loop in a Debug build tells you very little.
flags: compare the others against this one
toolkit.when: before you claim one pattern or API is faster than another

toolkit.what: CodeQL's security queries include js/redos and py/redos (exponential) and js/polynomial-redos and py/polynomial-redos (quadratic, like Stack Overflow's). GitHub code scanning runs them on every pull request.
flags: extract the code into a database first (python, csharp, java-kotlin too)
the standard pack for another language
output that code scanning and editors read
toolkit.example: codeql database create db --language=python && codeql database analyze db codeql/python-queries --format=sarif-latest --output=py.sarif
toolkit.when: in CI, so a vulnerable pattern is flagged in review

toolkit.what: ripgrep's default engine is Rust's regex crate (like RE2 and Go's regexp): finite automata, linear time on any input, so no pattern can hang it. The price: no lookarounds or backreferences.
flags: use PCRE2 for lookarounds and backreferences: a backtracking engine again
the default engine, switching to PCRE2 only when the pattern needs it
toolkit.when: searching huge or untrusted files: stay on the default engine when you can

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it gives you.
pairs: CPU, GC and thread pool numbers, live
a snapshot of every thread in the process
the managed stack of each thread in a dump
a sample of which methods used the CPU over time
ripgrep switched to PCRE2, a backtracking engine
a CodeQL query for exponential regexes

steps.prompt: The signup pod is at 100% CPU. Complete the commands: watch it live, take a dump, then open it.
code: # open the dump and print the stacks
steps.explain: In the stacks, look for the same `System.Text.RegularExpressions` frames on several threads, under the same method of yours. That method's pattern is the one to fix.

steps.title: Compile a customer's filter safely
prompt: Your log product lets customers type their own regex filters. You cannot rewrite their patterns, so make the engine
safe instead. Write `Regex? CompileUserFilter(string pattern)`:
- Build the regex with `RegexOptions.NonBacktracking` and a 100 ms match timeout (`TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100)`),
so no pattern can take more than linear time and nothing can run forever.
- Return `null` when the pattern is invalid (`ArgumentException`; `RegexParseException` derives from it) or needs a
feature NonBacktracking does not support (`NotSupportedException`), so the UI can say "pattern not supported".
`System.Text.RegularExpressions` is imported.
template: using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
{{CODE}}
Dojo.Try("a simple filter compiles", () =>
var dojoF = CompileUserFilter("error|fatal");
Dojo.Check("a simple filter compiles", dojoF is not null, "returned null");
Dojo.Eq("it matches 'fatal: disk full'", true, dojoF!.IsMatch("fatal: disk full"));
Dojo.Eq("it uses NonBacktracking", true, dojoF.Options.HasFlag(RegexOptions.NonBacktracking));
Dojo.Eq("it has a 100 ms timeout", TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100), dojoF.MatchTimeout);
Dojo.Try("(a+)+$ on 5,000 a and ! (timed out or threw)", () =>
var dojoBad = CompileUserFilter("(a+)+$");
Dojo.Eq("(a+)+$ on 5,000 a and ! answers false, fast", false, dojoBad!.IsMatch(new string('a', 5000) + "!"));
Dojo.Check("a backreference is refused", CompileUserFilter(@"(\w)\1") is null, "expected null");
Dojo.Check("a lookbehind is refused", CompileUserFilter(@"(?<=id=)[0-9]+") is null, "expected null");
Dojo.Check("a broken pattern is refused", CompileUserFilter("(") is null, "expected null");
hints: Two catch blocks, `ArgumentException` and `NotSupportedException`, each returning `null`.
